4 months is still a pretty short time in the big picture. I have a rule of thumb timeline for relationships. There are critical points the crop up at fairly common intervals.

0 months - Start

6 months - shiny newness begins to dissipate. Find out if you actually like the person, not the newness

1 year - If you make it past 1 year, the relationship will continue to 2 years.

2 years - 1st major make it or break it point. Large, explicit issues need to be resolved or a breakup will occur

5 years - Relationship has settled into "routine", and both partners may feel like they want a change of pace. Both partners should actively avoid the laziness of this period and work to truly appreciate their partner for who they are.

7 years - 2nd major make it or break it. Deep and fundamental character issues between two people must be resolved at this point or a breakup will occur. This is also a time when marriage becomes a big issue if not already married.

10 years - At this point, if the couple hasn't already been married, they are going to break up sometime soon. Only exception is if both people have been anti-marriage from the start. In that case, marriage will never have been an issue.

Personally, I enjoyed the film. As with all movies, it has its flaws. Unlike with most films, this one had the unfortunate fate of being directed by Zack Snyder, who is infamous for being terrible in the editing room. His other films, such as Watchmen and Sucker Punch, had amazing potential, but were directed by a gentleman with more style than substance.

The fight scenes, which are admittedly Zack's forte, were excellent. His stylized edits and direction really work for him in scenes that are action packed, but not as much outside of that. His use of shaky camera-work in certain scenes of the film were distracting at best, and detracted from the quality of the film in some places.

While many directors have their strengths, they also have their weaknesses, and Zack's is dialogue. Getting the actors he's working with to illicit emotion is something he seems to have a very hard time doing. Ben Affleck and Henry Cavil are both excellent actors, and have no trouble portraying what their characters might be feeling. Gal Gadot's performance, however, was wooden as a twenty year old mannequin. Every line she delivered was stiff, and lacking in emotion. Even her battle cry was bland. The easiest thing to do is shout in a primal manner that shows the rage one feels in combat, and even that felt flat.

Then there was Lex, portrayed by Jesse Eisenberg. His performance is best described as The Riddler masquerading as the cold-hearted bastard that many of us know and love as one of DC's most infamous villains. With his stuttering delivery, and the manner in which he spoke, all reminiscent of the green suited master of puzzles, my only though was "That's not Lex Luthor." Some say that's because Luthor's a genius, so I cannot comprehend his speech, but I never had that problem reading the comics. I never had that problem with the '90s cartoon. No, it's not that I can't understand him. It's that we saw the wrong character. Mr. Eisenburg is not a bad actor at all, and I honestly blame the writing and the directing more than I blame him.

Lastly, my biggest issue with the film, and why I say Zack Snyder is awful in the editing room, is the ending. Twenty minutes after the defeat of the "surprise" villain, we watch the funeral of Superman. Because he's definitely dead guys. Did you know Superman died? Guys, guys, let me tell you just how dead Superman is! Hey, we should form a group of metahumans and fight in Superman's memory! Did I mention he's dead? Yeah, that super guy died as a martyr for humanity. Oh, we're about half a minute from the credits? Guess what guys! Superman's not dead! Ha! Really had you going huh?

Zack, this is a personal message to you now. We get it. Superman fought Doomsday and "died" just like he did at the end of "The Death of Superman". Guess what we also know? I'm just gonna give you a minute to think on that.

...

...

Don't know it? Okay. I'll tell you. WE KNOW SUPERMAN'S NOT DEAD. HE CAN'T DIE ON EARTH. HE LITERALLY FLIES TO THE CENTER OF THE SUN AND BECOMES A GOD. Spending twenty minutes saying "He's really dead guys!" was a waste of the audience's time, and the very ending was a slap to the face regarding our intelligence. Whoever told you this was okay was wrong.

Regardless, those are my issues with the film. Despite them, I did manage to enjoy it, because what was good was really excellent. The fight scenes, Ben Affleck as Batman, the way that Superman was vilified while still being somebody I could identify with, these things made the film what it was for me. A popcorn flick, with good action, Batman and Superman, and a fight between the two. The sound engineering, the effects, the props, these things were amazing, and I wish director Zack Snyder would focus on those things, because he's REALLY GOOD at them. If nothing else, I feel as though a future project with Zack should have him just in charge of those, while a better director takes the lead.

My rating for the film is about a 7/10, because what was bad was terrible, but what was good was really good. Definitely worth seeing in theaters once, and I'll probably buy the disk when it comes out.
By the way, are there any reviews that try to judge the film from multiple different perspectives?
